question: Flora the frog starts at \(0\) on the number line and makes a sequence of jumps to the right. In any one jump, independent of previous jumps, Flora leaps a positive integer distance \(m\) with probability \(\dfrac{1}{2^m}.\) What is the probability that Flora will eventually land at \(10?\)
solution:
Every jump sequence that reaches \(10\) has the same probability, because its jump lengths add to \(10\). This lets us count successful sequences instead of calculating their probabilities separately.

Suppose Flora reaches \(10\) with successive jump lengths \(m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_k\). Independence gives the probability of this initial sequence as
\[
\frac{1}{2^{m_1}}\frac{1}{2^{m_2}}\cdots\frac{1}{2^{m_k}}
=\frac{1}{2^{m_1+\cdots+m_k}}
=\frac{1}{2^{10}}.
\]
Her later jumps are unrestricted.

To count these histories, choose which of the integers \(1,2,\ldots,9\) Flora lands on before reaching \(10\). Each integer can either be included or omitted, giving \(2^9\) subsets. Each subset determines exactly one jump sequence: list its elements in increasing order between \(0\) and \(10\), then take consecutive differences. Conversely, every successful sequence gives exactly one such subset.

These successful histories are mutually exclusive, since all jumps are positive and Flora cannot return to \(10\). Therefore their probabilities add, giving
\[
P(\text{eventually landing at }10)
=2^9\cdot\frac{1}{2^{10}}
=\boxed{\frac12},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
After the first jump, Flora faces the same problem with a smaller remaining distance. We can therefore relate the probabilities of reaching consecutive integers.

Let \(p_n\) be the probability of ever reaching \(n\) from \(0\), and set \(p_0=1\). If the first jump has length \(m\le n\), the probability of subsequently reaching \(n\) is \(p_{n-m}\), because future jumps are independent and follow the same rule. A first jump longer than \(n\) makes success impossible. Thus
\[
p_n=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\frac{p_{n-m}}{2^m}.
\]
For \(n\ge2\), separate the first term and shift the index in the remaining sum:
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_n
&=\frac{p_{n-1}}2+\sum_{m=2}^{n}\frac{p_{n-m}}{2^m}\\
&=\frac{p_{n-1}}2+\frac12\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\frac{p_{n-1-j}}{2^j}\\
&=\frac{p_{n-1}}2+\frac{p_{n-1}}2
=p_{n-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last sum is precisely the recurrence for \(p_{n-1}\).

Flora can reach \(1\) only by jumping \(1\) immediately, so \(p_1=\tfrac12\). Consequently,
\[
p_{10}=p_9=\cdots=p_1=\boxed{\frac12},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
solutionMethods.label: Compare consecutive hitting probabilities

solutionMethods.explanation:
From any position below \(10\), the probability that the next jump lands exactly at \(10\) equals the probability that it goes past \(10\). This balances the two possible ways Flora can first reach or pass the target.

If the remaining distance is the positive integer \(r\), then
\[
P(\text{next jump lands at }10)=\frac{1}{2^r}.
\]
Meanwhile, the probability of jumping farther than \(r\) is the geometric sum
\[
\sum_{m=r+1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^m}
=\frac{2^{-(r+1)}}{1-\frac12}
=\frac{1}{2^r}.
\]
For each possible jump history that stays below \(10\), multiply these equal probabilities by the probability of that history. This gives equal contributions to landing exactly at \(10\) and crossing past it on the next jump. Summing over all possible histories preserves the equality. There is no double counting, because each trajectory has a unique first jump that reaches or passes \(10\).

Since every jump is at least \(1\), that crossing occurs within at most \(10\) jumps. Landing exactly and overshooting therefore exhaust the possibilities, and each has probability
\[
\boxed{\frac12},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
solutionMethods.label: Balance landing and overshooting
